name: KLOW Protocol
lead: KLOW is a four-peptide research blend that circulates in peptide and biohacking communities. It combines GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV, and extends the earlier three-peptide GLOW stack with KPV. People discuss it for skin quality, hair, inflammation and recovery, which they link to looking better: smoother, firmer, calmer skin and faster recovery between training sessions. [1]

The components are described by promoters as follows: GHK-Cu for collagen and skin remodelling, KPV for calming inflammatory skin conditions such as acne and eczema, and BPC-157 and TB-500 for tissue repair.

The blend is not an approved drug, and the promoter material cited presents no controlled human trial of the combination has been published. Most of the underlying research on individual components is in cell or animal models. [1]

chain: Four peptides taken together by injection
Claimed to support collagen, calm inflammation and aid tissue repair
Clearer, firmer-looking skin and faster recovery
angle.text: Users take the blend hoping for better skin, hair and recovery. The skin case rests mainly on GHK-Cu, a peptide already used in cosmetics for firming, and KPV for inflammation, as described by promoters.

paras: A commonly listed vial contains GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. KPV is a short peptide derived from alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone; TB-500 is a thymosin beta-4 derivative; GHK-Cu is a copper-binding peptide; BPC-157 is a stable gastric peptide fragment. [1]

GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring copper complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine, isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart and a colleague in 1973. Synthetic GHK-Cu is used in cosmetics as a reparative and anti-ageing ingredient under the INCI name Copper tripeptide-1, and in hair-loss-prevention products. [2] Wikipedia reports several controlled facial studies describing firming and anti-wrinkle effects, noting small sample sizes and short durations. [2]

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide derived from a protein in human gastric juice, discovered by Predrag Sikirić of the University of Zagreb and reported in 1993. Most studies are in laboratory animals, with preclinical reports of tissue-healing and anti-inflammatory effects, and human evidence is very limited. It is not approved by drug regulators for human use and is banned by WADA. [3]

TB-500 is described by promoters as a thymosin beta-4 derivative and KPV as a short fragment related to alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone; promoter material credits KPV with calming inflammatory skin conditions. [1]

Promoters describe skin benefits (collagen, elastin, acne and dermatitis), hair growth from GHK-Cu, and faster recovery from training injuries from BPC-157 and TB-500. One promoter reports his own acne improving; such accounts are anecdotal. [1]

No studies found on the KLOW blend. Research on individual components: GHK-Cu has controlled facial studies of small size and short duration, [2] while BPC-157 evidence is largely from animal studies with very limited human data. [3]
The blend is not an approved drug and is marketed as a research product. The promoter page cited here presents no safety data for the blend or its individual peptides. [1]

Wikipedia notes that BPC-157 promotes angiogenesis, which has raised theoretical concerns about cancer, and that health authorities discourage its use because human safety data are insufficient. [3] It adds that GHK-Cu stimulates both collagen synthesis and enzymes that break down dermal proteins, so caution is advised. [2]

timeline.event: Loren Pickart isolates GHK-Cu from human plasma. [2]

lore.intro: KLOW is promoted by peptide vendors and newsletters as an upgrade of the GLOW stack. [1]

claims.claim: The four peptides work better together for skin and recovery
claims.believers: Promoters say each peptide covers a different pathway: collagen, inflammation and tissue repair. [1]
claims.experts: The promoter page presents no study of the combination; synergy is asserted rather than tested.

claims.claim: GHK-Cu grows hair comparably to minoxidil
claims.believers: A promoter states this without naming trials. [1]
claims.experts: The cited page names no trials for the blend. [1]

card.summary: A GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV peptide blend that people use hoping for clearer skin, hair support and faster recovery.
card.note: Not an approved drug; no human trials of the combination cited.

quick.overview:
KLOW is a four-peptide blend: GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. It builds on the GLOW stack by adding KPV, and is discussed for skin quality, hair and recovery.

It is sold by research-peptide vendors, typically as a single vial, and is discussed largely in biohacking newsletters.
quick.mechanism: Promoters attribute collagen and skin remodelling to GHK-Cu, anti-inflammatory action to KPV, and tissue repair to BPC-157 and TB-500. These mechanisms are drawn from cell and animal research on the individual peptides.
quick.risks: The blend is not an approved drug and no human trial of it is cited by promoters. Promotional material presents no safety data for the combination.
